text:
About Me
I am an undergraduate student in Genomic Sciences at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), guided by humanity, ressponsibility and accountability.
My main interests include:

Immunology and host–virus interactions.

Neuroscience, particularly neurodevelopment and neurodegenerative diseases.

Bioinformatics & Genomics, especially RNA-seq and machine learning applications in biology.

I combine my background in biology with bioinformatics skills to understand biological phenomena and address questions about life from different perspectives. I am also developing skills in project and business management, with the goal of connecting scientific knowledge with real-world applications in biotechnology.
My commitment is to contribute to impactful research by turning scientific questions into meaningful insights and solutions.

title: Research
text: My research focuses on leveraging single-cell genomics, transcriptomics, and population genetics to understand human genetic diversity, cell-type-specific regulation, and complex traits across diverse populations.

title: Research
text:
Current Research Projects

Single-Cell Population Genomics
Focus: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis of Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells (PBMCs) from indigenous populations of Colombia.

Goal: Characterize cell-type-specific transcriptomic variation and immune diversity in underrepresented Latin American populations.
Methods: Pseudobulk aggregation, cell type annotation (Azimuth, MapMyCells), differential expression (edgeR, Seurat), and quality control workflows in R and Python.
Affiliation: MorenoLab (Cinvestav / LANGEBIO).




Human Brain & Neurogenomics
Focus: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic workflows in human brain tissue to map neurodevelopmental patterns and cellular diversity.

Goal: Investigate cell-type specific gene expression changes in brain regions and their association with neurodevelopmental contexts.
Methods: High-throughput single-cell data processing, reproducible workflows, and cluster execution using Slurm HPC environments.
Affiliation: Lieber Institute for Brain Development.

title: Research
text:

title: Fahrenheit 451: Memory, Critical Thought, and the Preservation of Knowledge
text:
Ray Bradbury’s Fahrenheit 451 is often read as a warning about government censorship, but its core theme runs much deeper: it warns against a society that willingly abandons literature and critical reflection in favor of immediate, frictionless distraction.
In Bradbury’s dystopian world, firemen do not extinguish fires; they burn books to maintain a superficial state of collective harmony.

title: Fahrenheit 451: Memory, Critical Thought, and the Preservation of Knowledge
text:
Key Takeaways & Personal Reflections

1. Speed, Noise, and Constant Distraction
Guy Montag’s world is defined by parlor walls and seashells—constant streams of noise that leave no quiet space for introspection. Bradbury foresaw how hyper-connectivity and immediate satisfaction can erode our capacity for sustained, deep thought.


2. The Living Books
One of the most powerful concepts in the novel is the community of outcasts who memorize entire literary and philosophical works to preserve them for future generations. Knowledge is no longer stored on paper, but within human memory and oral tradition.


3. Science and Literature
Working in scientific research often requires deep technical focus, but engaging with literature like Fahrenheit 451 provides a vital counterweight—reminding us of the human contexts, ethics, and histories that give direction to our analytical work.

Recommended for anyone interested in classic dystopian fiction, philosophy of technology, and the history of ideas.

title: Pseudobulk Aggregation Workflows for Single-Cell RNA-seq Data
text:
When analyzing single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets, treating individual cells as independent statistical replicates can lead to inflated false-positive rates due to cell-to-cell dependencies within the same biological sample.
Aggregating single-cell counts into pseudobulk profiles by sample and cell type allows us to leverage well-established bulk differential expression frameworks (like edgeR or DESeq2).

title: Pseudobulk Aggregation Workflows for Single-Cell RNA-seq Data
section: Key Steps in Pseudobulk Differential Expression
text:
Key Steps in Pseudobulk Differential Expression

Cell Type Annotation & QC: Ensure low-quality cells and doublets are removed prior to aggregation.
Aggregation by Sample & Cell Type: Sum unnormalized raw counts for each gene within each combination of cell type and donor sample.
Statistical Testing: Model counts using negative binomial generalized linear models (GLMs).

# Load necessary libraries
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(Seurat)
  library(edgeR)
  library(dplyr)
})

# Example: Aggregating raw counts in Seurat v5
# pbmc is a Seurat object with 'cell_type' and 'donor_id' in meta.data
pseudobulk_counts <- AggregateExpression(
  object = pbmc,
  group.by = c("cell_type", "donor_id"),
  slot = "counts"
)

# Inspect aggregated matrix for a specific cell type
head(pseudobulk_counts$RNA)
